clue.text: see 4dn.
see 26dn.
Reputation of peer involving Tories useless leaders

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one word wraps round the other letters

parts.note: to peer is to look hard, to stare

indicators.note: leaders are those at the front, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A peer's standing among the Tories, who are portrayed as being led by useless people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a lord, which suits the Tories; here it is the verb meaning to look closely.
explanation.definitionFit: Stature in the figurative sense is standing or prestige, a synonym for reputation.

clue.text: (& 1dn.) Private Eye will stuff outside independent fat cat's modest description?

parts.note: the magazine speaking of itself: we will, contracted to we'll

indicators.note: the stuffing word goes outside, so it wraps round the letter for independent

parts.note: to stuff is to pad
I is the standard abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: Private Eye vows to stuff a fat cat who calls himself independent and modest.
explanation.walkthrough: The magazine habitually speaks of itself as 'we', so 'Private Eye will' is the contraction we'll, minus its apostrophe in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A fat cat earning a vast salary would understate it as merely being paid well, a sly understatement.

clue.text: The business that connects one with low-down duck's arse

parts.note: one is the indefinite article a
gen is slang for information, the low-down
DA is short for duck's arse, a 1950s greased-back hairstyle

explanation.surface: Something rude about linking someone with a duck's backside and gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck's arse, or DA, is a quiff-style haircut swept back to look like a duck's tail.
explanation.definitionFit: An agenda is the list of items, the business, to be dealt with at a meeting.

clue.text: see 21dn.
(& 18ac.) Sponsor France's main intervention in leak about Sarkozy's unlikely partner?

parts.note: an angel is a financial backer, especially of a stage show

indicators.note: an intervention comes between, so these letters are placed inside the others
turned about means moved around, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the main is the sea, which is mer in French

explanation.surface: A sponsor's role in a leak story about Nicolas Sarkozy's improbable companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like the adjective; it is the old word for the sea, and 'France's' asks for it in French.
explanation.definitionFit: The German chancellor and the French president worked closely as a pair, nicknamed Merkozy, an odd couple.

clue.text: Bollocks? Saw off for laughs

parts.note: guff is nonsense, rubbish talk

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone cries nonsense and says they sawed something off just for a laugh.
explanation.definitionFit: Guffaws are loud, hearty bursts of laughter, so the plural noun matches laughs.

clue.text: Given rein, most politicians will go on this

definitions.text: Given rein, most politicians will go on this

parts.words: Given rein, most politicians will go on this
parts.note: surface reading: a horse given its head goes on a long lead or tether

parts.words: most politicians will go on this
parts.note: setter's reading: given free rein, politicians talk endlessly, going on and on for a long time

explanation.walkthrough: Rein and tether suggest a length of rope; the idiom is to go on, speaking without stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak at length is to talk for a long time, which is what a long-winded politician does.

clue.text: "Eden? F-off!" — day TV presenter who's in the dock

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters before it are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for day
Ant McPartlin, half of the British TV presenting duo Ant and Dec

explanation.surface: A daytime TV host tells Anthony Eden to get lost, then lands up in court.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude 'F-off!' hides the anagram signal; Ant is one of Ant and Dec, the British TV presenters.
explanation.definitionFit: A defendant is the person accused in a trial, who stands in the dock of a courtroom.

clue.text: see 14dn.
Extreme Left-winger Neil Kinnock's heart broken

indicators.note: something broken has its parts scattered, so the letters are reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so only the middle letter of the surname is used

parts.note: the fourth of seven letters sits in the middle

explanation.surface: A hard-left figure says Labour leader Neil Kinnock's heart is broken.
explanation.walkthrough: Neil Kinnock led the British Labour Party in the 1980s and fought its hard left.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenin led the Bolshevik revolution, a figure on the far, revolutionary wing of politics.

clue.text: Spooks from Washington protecting Republican shit organisation

indicators.note: to protect is to shield by surrounding, so the state's letters go round the next

parts.note: WA is the postal abbreviation for Washington state
R is the abbreviation for Republican

indicators.note: organising puts things into a fresh order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Washington spies shielding a Republican and his dirty organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooks' in a Washington surface suggests CIA agents; here it means ghosts.
explanation.definitionFit: Wraiths are ghosts or apparitions, and spook is an informal word for a ghost.

clue.text: Slanging match following articles LibDem leader removed from sci-fi classic

indicators.note: removed means taken away, so these letters are cut out of the title

parts.note: H. G. Wells's novel of a Martian invasion
the definite article, twice over in the title

indicators.note: a leader goes first, so only the opening letter of the party name is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the party name

explanation.surface: A row breaks out after the Liberal Democrat leader is cut from a science-fiction film.
explanation.walkthrough: The full title has two THEs, hence 'articles' plural; the L goes from WORLDS.
explanation.definitionFit: A war of words is an angry exchange of insults, the same thing as a slanging match.

clue.text: (& 11dn.) Scrooge pissed with Bottom

parts.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, as is tight
arse is British slang for the bottom

explanation.surface: Ebenezer Scrooge drunk alongside Bottom, the weaver from A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English pissed means drunk, not angry.
explanation.definitionFit: A tightarse is a mean, stingy person, and Scrooge is the byword for a miser.

clue.text: Brenda taken aback: "One's removed from one's residence (as one's son would to do to one)"

definitions.text: as one's son would to do to one

indicators.note: taken aback suggests being pushed backwards, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: Brenda is Private Eye's name for the Queen, Elizabeth Regina, ER

indicators.note: removed from means taken out of, so a letter leaves the word

parts.note: the Queen lives in a palace
one is the article a

explanation.surface: The Queen is shocked at the idea of being evicted from Buckingham Palace, as her son would do.
explanation.walkthrough: The regal 'one' is the joke; the son is Charles, who would succeed her. The clue's 'to do' is a printed slip for 'do'.
explanation.definitionFit: An heir succeeds a monarch, taking their place on the throne, which is to replace them.

clue.text: Mangle hacks!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: squeeze flat, as a mangle wrings laundry

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an order to maul journalists; mangle here is the laundry wringer sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To press is to squeeze flat like a mangle, and the press is the body of journalists or hacks.

clue.text: Peres ignored accommodating surrender

indicators.note: to accommodate is to house, so the words hold the answer inside them

parts.note: runs across the two words

explanation.surface: Shimon Peres was ignored when he offered to make concessions.
explanation.definitionFit: To resign is to give up or yield, as a chess player resigns a lost game, which is surrender.

clue.text: see 7ac.
Dicky's after top way to dump soap character?

definitions.note: noun phrase for a verb: killing off is the way

parts.note: to top is slang for to kill
dicky is British slang for unwell or faulty, off

explanation.surface: An ailing actor is after the top role, a way to get rid of a soap opera character.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky, as in a dicky heart, is British slang for weak or unreliable.
explanation.definitionFit: Soap writers remove an unwanted character by having them die in the plot.

clue.text: No need to press a wet (not what he ought to be)

parts.note: a wet is a feeble person, a drip

parts.words: not what he ought to be
parts.note: the opposite of wet, which a wet ought not to be

explanation.surface: No need to lean on a feeble Tory moderate, who is not what he should be.
explanation.walkthrough: Under Thatcher, moderate Tories were wets and hardliners dries; the wet is told he should be dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Drip-dry fabric is hung up wet and dries without creases, so ironing is unnecessary.

clue.text: (& 6dn.) "Heavy metal" Osborne's butch description of 7/18?

parts.note: iron is a dense metal
George Osborne was Chancellor of the Exchequer

explanation.surface: A rock music tag for George Osborne's macho label for the German leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The Iron Chancellor was Bismarck's nickname; Merkel, also a German chancellor, inherited it in the press.
explanation.definitionFit: A hard-sounding nickname for a female German head of government echoes Bismarck's tough, masculine image.

clue.text: Her gift: screwing a soldier

indicators.note: screwing means twisting, so the letters are turned into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman's present to a serviceman is going to bed with him.
explanation.definitionFit: A fighter is a combatant, someone who fights, as a soldier does.

clue.text: Sizeable testicle appears round foot of bed

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: gooly or goolie is British slang for a testicle

indicators.note: the foot is the bottom end, so only the last letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A large testicle shows up at the bottom of the bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Goolies is British slang for testicles.
explanation.definitionFit: Goodly is an old word for considerable in size or amount, as in a goodly sum.

clue.text: Criminal nuts lust after Queen Brenda

indicators.note: after places the jumbled word behind the royal letter rather than before it

parts.note: R is short for Regina, queen

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters beside it are rearranged wildly

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
Brenda is Private Eye's name for the Queen, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A criminal crazed with desire for the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the jumbled word after the R; Private Eye has long called the Queen Brenda.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustler is a thief of livestock, so a kind of criminal.

clue.text: Wham-bam-thank-you-ma'am guy's sort of relationship?

parts.note: surface reading: a man after quick sex with no aftercare
setter's reading: a fling that stops and starts, read literally as he gets on and gets straight off

explanation.walkthrough: A wham-bam lover climbs on and climbs straight off, which literally describes the familiar term for an intermittent romance.
explanation.definitionFit: An intermittent relationship that keeps breaking up and resuming is described with this hyphenated pair of opposites.

clue.text: (& 28/2) In a flap with every pisspoor grandiose political scheme

indicators.note: pisspoor means wretchedly bad, so the letters are in a poor, jumbled order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Panicking over each badly conceived, overblown government project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a flap' looks like a state of panic; it is just letters for the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Soviet-style five-year plans were ambitious state economic programmes, the classic overreaching political scheme.

clue.text: Tories, say, needing time to replace Right and water down members' cover-up

indicators.note: to replace is to swap one thing for another, so one letter stands in for another

parts.note: the Tories are an example of a political party
T is the abbreviation for time
R is the abbreviation for right
to hose down is to wash with water

explanation.surface: The Tories dilute a scandal about their members, given time.
explanation.walkthrough: As printed, putting T for R in PARTY gives PATTY; the grid needs N, so the swap only works if the incoming letter is N. Members are legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantyhose, the American word for tights, cover the legs, which are limbs or members.

clue.text: see 26dn.

clue.text: Labour's ultimate goal turned Miliband slightly ill?

indicators.note: turned means facing the other way, so the leader's name is read backwards

parts.note: Ed Miliband, then Labour leader
livery is an old word for liverish, mildly unwell

explanation.surface: Labour's aim made Ed Miliband feel a bit queasy.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the labour of childbirth, not the Labour Party. Ed Miliband led Labour from 2010 to 2015.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour in childbirth ends with the birth of the baby, which is the delivery.

clue.text: One at the top who's prone to cock up public statements?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the boss or foreman

definitions.text: who's prone to cock up public statements
definitions.meaning: second meaning, whimsically: someone who makes gaffes

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is invented: a gaffer as one who makes gaffes, embarrassing slips.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaffer is British informal for a boss or manager, and a gaffe is a public blunder.
